corrected_value.title: Now you see it, now you don’t: On turning semantic interference into facilitation in a Stroop-like task.

decision.location: Experiment 2, Results and discussion (lines 555-562); see also Experiment 2 introduction (lines 425-429), Experiment 2 discussion (lines 579-582), and References (lines 893-894)
decision.quote:
We
introduced a control condition, in which distractors and picture were semantically related. If
distractors are not processed under masked conditions, no effect should be found with
semantically related distractors either. However, a semantic facilitation effect was present. As
stimuli were presented under the same masking and timing parameters in both conditions, it
seems unlikely that the same subjects could only process the distractors when they were
semantically related to the target. Also, the same semantic facilitation effect was found by
Finkbeiner & Caramazza (2006) who used the same presentation parameters as we did.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Experiment 2 (N = 40 Dutch speakers), Dhooge and Hartsuiker empirically retest the finding of Finkbeiner and Caramazza (2006) that picture-word interference with semantically related vs. unrelated distractors produces semantic interference when distractors are visible but reverses into semantic facilitation when distractors are masked using the same presentation timing parameters. Experiment 2 tests the relatedness by visibility interaction (F1(1,39) = 26.62, p < .001; F2(1,19) = 17.57, p < .001), confirms both visible semantic interference and masked semantic facilitation, explicitly compares the finding with Finkbeiner and Caramazza (2006), and states that 'by replicating the semantic facilitation effect, this experiment also provides further evidence for a non-competitive model of lexical selection.' The reference list (lines 893-894) identifies the primary study as 'Finkbeiner, M., & Caramazza, A. (2006). Now you see it, now you don’t: On turning semantic interference into facilitation in a Stroop-like task. Cortex, 42, 790–796.' (distinct from the 2006b reply commentary on lines 895-896), with no DOI printed in the source text. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 663, 10.1037/0096-3445.132.2.228, Miozzo & Caramazza, 2003, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 132, 228-252) represents the unmasked distractor-frequency original retested in Experiment 1 (sibling target_index 0). Because Finkbeiner and Caramazza (2006) is an independent study in Cortex testing a different empirical phenomenon (masked reversal of semantic interference into facilitation), report equivalence does not apply and the target is genuinely absent from the shipped rows. Luna's invalid table-formatted duplicate_quote was discarded and replaced with a verified contiguous primary-source quote preserving exact line breaks.

decision.quote: The well‐known study by Leiponen and Helfat (2010) examined how firms increased their odds of innovation success by pursuing multiple parallel innovation objectives and knowledge sources. We replicate their study across geographic and temporal contexts using three sets of data: from Finland ( N = 884) in 2006–2008 and from other European countries in two different time periods ( N = 36,480 in 2006–2008 and 24,326 in 2008–2010).

corrected_value.title: Habituation and dishabituation to speech and office noise.

decision.location: Experiment 1, Discussion (lines 756-767); see also Experiment 1 introduction (lines 392-440, 495-528), Results (lines 674-702), and References (lines 1557-1559)
decision.quote:
The results from this study support
the findings from Banbury and Berry[14] showing that office

noise can disrupt performance on working memory tasks (i.e.

mental arithmetic) but that this disruption can be habituated

to after a period of time in noise. This study has gone on

to show that participants fully habituated to the office noise

following 10 minutes intervening exposure.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Experiment 1 (N = 36 undergraduates), Smith, Waters, and Jones empirically retest the laboratory finding of Banbury and Berry (1997, ref. 14) that background office noise with speech initially disrupts cognitive task performance and that prior exposure to office noise produces habituation that removes this disruption (testing 5-minute habituation blocks up to 20 minutes). Experiment 1 finds a significant noise condition by habituation block interaction (F(8,132) = 4, p < 0.05) with initial impairment in office noise eliminated after 10 minutes of prior exposure, and the Discussion explicitly compares these results to Banbury and Berry [14]. Reference 14 in the bibliography (lines 1557-1559) provides the exact identity: 'Banbury S, Berry DC. Habituation and dishabituation to speech and office noise. J Exp Psychol Appl 1997;3:181-95.' with no DOI printed in the source text. The only shipped row for this work is input_row_index 665 (10.1038/365611a0, Rauscher, Shaw, & Ky, 1993, 'Music and spatial task performance', Nature, 365, 611), which is the Mozart effect original tested in Experiment 2 (sibling target_index 1), and sibling target_index 2 is Thompson et al. (2001). Because Banbury and Berry (1997) is an independent study by different authors on office-noise habituation, report equivalence does not apply and it is genuinely absent from all shipped rows.

corrected_value.title: Arousal, mood, and the Mozart effect.

decision.location: Experiment 2, Discussion (lines 1373-1380); see also Experiment 2 introduction (lines 1117-1168), Results (lines 1339-1360), and References (lines 1663-1665)
decision.quote:
There was evidence to suggest that the Mozart

effect is not due to positive mood arousal as suggested by

Chabris[38] and Thompson et al.[36] Indeed, the mood ratings

showed no evidence that listening to Mozart increased
alertness or hedonic tone.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Experiment 2 (N = 24 undergraduates in a within-subjects design), Smith, Waters, and Jones empirically retest the published finding of Thompson, Schellenberg, and Husain (2001, ref. 36) that listening to Mozart's Sonata K448 increases positive arousal and mood ratings and that the Mozart effect on spatial-temporal performance is explained by positive arousal and mood. Experiment 2 directly measures participants' mood ratings (alertness, hedonic tone, and anxiety) before and after listening to Mozart K448, a positive mood induction, and silence alongside spatial-temporal performance on the RMPFB test, finding no effect of Mozart on alertness or hedonic tone and superior spatial performance after Mozart relative to both silence and mood induction, and explicitly concludes against Thompson et al. [36] (whereas Chabris [38] is explicitly described on lines 966-969 as a meta-analysis and excluded under the codebook). Reference 36 (lines 1663-1665) provides the literal source citation: 'Thompson WF, Scbellenberg EG, Husain G. Arousal, mood, and the Mozart effect. Psychol Sci 2001;12:248-51.' (with the literal transcription 'Scbellenberg EG' in the reference list and no DOI printed). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 665, 10.1038/365611a0, Rauscher, Shaw, & Ky, 1993, Nature, 365, 611) represents the original Mozart spatial-performance study (sibling target_index 1), while sibling target_index 0 is Banbury and Berry (1997). Thompson et al. (2001) is an independent empirical article in Psychological Science by different authors, so report equivalence does not apply and it is genuinely absent from the shipped rows.
